opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting open questions, and I should say up front that a lot of what I'll describe is still more intuition than settled result.

The way I think about it, a continual-learning model has two very different jobs. During the "waking" phase, it's interacting with the world, taking in new tokens, and updating its fast-changing memory: the parts of the system that adapt at test time. That memory is great for capturing what's happening right now, but it's limited in capacity and it's noisy. It's storing a lot of surprising, specific things without much consolidation.

The "sleep" phase is when you'd want to move what matters out of that short-term, high-plasticity memory into the slower, more persistent parameters, without destroying what's already there. That's basically the catastrophic forgetting problem framed in a more biological way.

Dreaming, in that picture, is the mechanism that makes consolidation safe. If you only replay the new experiences, you overwrite old knowledge. If you only rehearse old knowledge, you never integrate anything new. So what you want is a kind of generative replay: the model samples from its own internal distribution, mixing recent memories with older ones, recombining them, and training the slower layers on that mixture. It's interleaving, but the model generates the interleaved data itself rather than keeping a giant buffer of raw past data.

There are a few things I find compelling about that framing. First, it's a form of compression. You don't store everything; you store a model that can regenerate the important structure, and dreaming tests whether that structure is still there. Second, it gives you a natural place to do abstraction. When you recombine fragments of experience, you're implicitly asking, "What's the shared pattern here?" That's closer to how you'd want generalization to emerge, as opposed to memorizing individual episodes. Third, it can act as a kind of self-check. If the model's dreams start drifting into nonsense, that tells you something about where its memory is degrading.

And connecting it to the multi-timescale view of memory we've been working on: you can think of the system as having levels that update at different frequencies. Dreaming is the process that moves information across those levels, from the fast ones to the slow ones, in a way that's selective. Surprise or importance during waking decides what gets flagged, and sleep decides what actually gets written into long-term memory.

I don't want to overclaim that we have this working in a clean way at scale. But I do think the field has spent a lot of time on the waking half, meaning how to learn at test time, and much less on the offline consolidation half. That's where I expect a lot of the interesting progress to come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the dreaming analogy is actually one of the more useful ones here, as long as we're careful about it. When we talk about a sleep phase in a continual-learning system, the basic idea is that the model isn't just passively accumulating updates while it's awake, in context, and then freezing. There's a separate phase where it goes back over what it experienced and decides what actually deserves to be written into longer-term parameters.

Dreaming, in that framing, is the replay and recombination part of that. If you look at what the brain seems to do during sleep, it's not just storing a log of the day. It replays episodes, often in compressed or distorted form, it mixes them with older memories, and it seems to prioritize things that were surprising or emotionally salient. And that maps pretty directly onto what you'd want in a learning system. You don't want to consolidate everything at the same rate. You want to spend your gradient budget on the things that violated your expectations, because those are the things your current parameters are worst at predicting.

So in our work, the way I think about it is that during the awake phase, the fast memory, the in-context component, is absorbing information and making a kind of running estimate of how surprising each piece is. That surprise signal is really the key. Then in the sleep phase, you replay, and the replay is weighted by that signal. Things that were easy, things the model already predicted well, don't need to be rehearsed much. Things that were hard get rehearsed more, and get pushed into the slower, more persistent layers.

The recombination part is where it gets interesting and where I'd say we're more speculative. Biological dreams are generative. They take fragments of real experience and produce novel sequences. For a model, you could imagine the sleep phase not only replaying real sequences but sampling from the model itself, generating synthetic continuations, and then training on those. There's a risk there, obviously, which is that you end up amplifying your own errors, the model dreams up something wrong and then memorizes it. So you need something that keeps it grounded, some anchor to actual experience, or a way to discount self-generated samples relative to real ones. But if you get that balance right, it's a way to generalize beyond the exact data you saw. You're essentially doing data augmentation in a space the model itself has learned.

The other role I'd highlight is forgetting. People tend to think of consolidation as purely additive, but a big part of sleep in biology seems to be pruning, weakening connections that weren't reinforced. In a continual learner that's essential, because otherwise you just saturate. Memory capacity is finite, and if everything you ever saw stays at the same strength, eventually you can't write anything new without catastrophic interference. So I'd say dreaming is also where the system decides what it's allowed to let go of, and that decision is just as important as what it decides to keep.

So, to summarize, I see three functions. Selective replay driven by surprise, so you spend learning where it's needed. Recombination, so you generalize rather than just memorize. And pruning, so you have room to keep learning tomorrow. The nice thing is that all three of those are things you can actually write down as objectives and test, which is what makes the analogy more than just a metaphor to me.

astra-6.text:
I think dreaming could play the role of replay, but replay doesn’t necessarily mean reproducing exactly what the model experienced. It could mean generating variations of those experiences and using them to consolidate what it has learned.

In a continual-learning system, you’re constantly incorporating new information, and that can interfere with older knowledge. A sleep phase gives you an opportunity to revisit that knowledge without having to respond to new inputs at the same time. Dreaming could provide the internal experiences that drive that process: bringing together something you learned recently with something you learned much earlier, and finding structure that connects them.

The challenge is deciding what to dream about and what to reinforce. If the model simply trains on whatever it generates, it could reinforce its own mistakes. So I’d treat dreaming as a promising mechanism for consolidation and exploration, but one that needs a way to stay grounded in actual experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think dreaming could play the role of internally generated replay. When a model is learning continuously, its immediate experience is only a small slice of what it has learned. During sleep, it could revisit older knowledge, combine it with recent experience, and consolidate those connections without needing the original data in front of it.

The interesting possibility is that it doesn't just replay exact examples. It generates variations or combinations, which could help it generalize while preserving previous capabilities. But you need to be careful: if the model trains on its own mistakes, it can reinforce them. So the question is what constrains that process—what makes a generated experience useful for consolidation rather than a source of drift.

I would treat dreaming as a hypothesis for how to organize that internal learning, rather than assume that reproducing biological dreaming is necessary.
